tour.title: Palace, Market & the Campuhan Ridge
tour.summary: A royal town, a temple, an art revolution and a sacred river confluence — walking the heart of Bali's cultural capital from the palace to the Campuhan ridge.
tour.overviewText:
Ubud smells of frangipani and two-stroke engines, and the first thing to understand is that the island it sits on is not like the country around it. Indonesia is the world's most populous Muslim-majority nation, but Bali is the exception: about nine in ten Balinese are Hindu, practising a faith unlike anything in India. Balinese Hinduism layers Hindu gods with Buddhist ideas, ancestor veneration and older spirit worship, and it is a religion of daily, visible practice. You will meet it as a canang sari: a small tray woven from palm leaf, holding a few flowers, a pinch of rice and a burning stick of incense, set out each morning as an offering. The etiquette on this walk — sarongs, shoes off, voices down — is not fussiness. It is the price of walking through someone's worship.

The town is small and overwhelmed: about twelve thousand people in the central village, seventy-five thousand in the district, and millions of visitors a year. Two things made Ubud. The first is geography: it sits where two rivers meet at a place called Campuhan, a confluence the Balinese consider sacred, on ground the old texts call medicinal — ubad, in Balinese, is where the name Ubud comes from. The second is art. In the 1920s and 1930s Ubud's royal family invited foreign painters to live here. A German, Walter Spies, and a Dutchman, Rudolf Bonnet, arrived, and with the prince they founded an association called Pita Maha that turned village craft into a modern painting movement and sold the world its idea of "Bali". Palace, market and temple — the three things you walk between — are the machinery of that bargain, still running.

It is also a town that argues with itself. Tourism pays for almost everything, and it is eating the rice fields that tourists come to see: Bali loses roughly a thousand hectares of farmland a year, and tourism now consumes most of the island's freshwater. The irrigation cooperatives that built the terraces — the subak, a thousand years old and UNESCO-listed — are being squeezed. Supporters of the boom call it renewal and jobs; critics warn that tourism is killing the thing it sells. This walk puts you inside that argument rather than above it.

The route is simple. It starts at the royal palace, crosses to the art market, follows the road west through the water temple and Bali's first art museum, then drops south to the monkey forest and finishes on the Campuhan ridge above the river confluence. It is about four and a half kilometres and an hour of walking, mostly level, with one short ride — plus the ridge path itself, up to two kilometres more if you walk it to the far end.

Go early. Ubud is hot and humid year-round, and this walk is best started around 8am, before the coaches and the midday sun. Carry cash in rupiah, the Indonesian currency, cover your shoulders and knees for the temples, and check whether your dates collide with Nyepi, Bali's day of silence — in March 2027 it falls on the 8th, when the whole island shuts. Bring water; expect to be offered a sarong and a scooter ride at least once.

Ubud rewards the walker who looks past the souvenir stalls. Start walking.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. The palace, market, temple and museum sit within a few hundred metres of each other on flat pavement, but the pavement is broken in places and you dodge scooters. The monkey forest is gentle forest path with some steps, and the Campuhan ridge is a narrow concrete path with a steady climb and no shade at midday.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 8am, before the heat and the coach crowds. Do the palace, market, temple and museum in the cool morning, reach the monkey forest late morning when the macaques are active, then take a car to the Campuhan ridge for the last hour or two of golden light — the ridge is best in the early morning or the late afternoon, and there is no shade in between. On Nyepi the whole island is closed, so plan around it.

stops.name: Ubud Palace (Puri Saren Agung)
stops.narration:
Stop under the big banyan fig and look at the wall. This is Puri Saren Agung — the Great Palace of Saren — usually just called the Ubud Palace, and it has been the seat of Ubud's royal family since the early 1800s. A puri is a Balinese palace, and this one took its present shape under a king named Tjokorda Putu Kandel, who ruled from about 1800 to 1823. Tjokorda is the title of Ubud's royal line, the Sukawati dynasty, and the family still lives inside these walls, which is why some courtyards are closed and the place feels less like a museum than a house with very old, very public manners.

In 1917 an earthquake flattened much of it, and the family rebuilt. In 1928 they did something more radical: they opened the palace to paying foreign guests, making it one of Ubud's first hotels. That decision tells you how Ubud works. Royalty here has never been a museum piece; it is an economic actor. When tourist money arrived, the palace was already a landlord.

Look at the carved stone while you wait — much of it is the work of I Gusti Nyoman Lempad, a sculptor and architect who worked for the royal family for decades and whose name you will meet twice more on this walk. Then notice the plan. This is not one building but a compound of pavilions, shrines and gateways, and that open-courtyard layout is the basic grammar of Balinese architecture: a temple or a palace is a walled garden of small buildings, not one big hall.

Come back after dark and the courtyard fills with dancers. Balinese dance is not folk entertainment laid on for tourists; it is a temple art performed here for generations, and the palace is its best stage in Ubud. You will hear the gamelan first — the percussion orchestra of bronze metallophones, gongs and drums that gives every Balinese ceremony its pulse. Watch for Legong, the precise, trance-like dance of young girls, or Kecak, the "monkey chant", in which a chorus of men supplies the rhythm with their voices alone. Tickets start around Rp 75,000 and the money goes to the performers' village troupes — but verify the night's programme and price at the gate, because the shows rotate between the palace and the Saraswati temple.

Entry in daylight is free, roughly 09:00 to 17:00; parts of the compound are off-limits because the family lives here, and if you enter a temple courtyard you will need a sarong, a length of cloth wrapped round the waist, and a sash. Bring small rupiah notes for the evening show. Now cross the road to the market.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free in daylight. Evening dance performances are ticketed, from around Rp 75,000 — programmes and prices rotate, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 09:00 to 17:00 for the public courtyards; some areas are closed because the royal family lives on site. Evening dance shows usually start around 19:30. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Level paved courtyard at the entrance with a few low steps between pavilions. The ground is uneven stone in places. Wheelchairs can manage the main courtyard but not the whole compound.
stops.insiderTip: Come back at night for the dance — the gamelan and the floodlit gate are worth the ticket. In daylight, look at the stone carving by the entrance, much of it by I Gusti Nyoman Lempad, the sculptor you will also meet at the water temple and the art museum.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross Jalan Raya Ubud to the market building directly opposite — about a hundred metres. Pasar Seni Ubud, the art market, is the two-storey block on the far corner, its upper floor hidden behind hanging sarongs.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ubud Art Market (Pasar Seni Ubud)
stops.narration:
Step into the noise. This is Pasar Seni Ubud — pasar is Indonesian for market, seni means art — and it is the commercial heart of a town that sells itself. The building is a double-storey warren of stalls, and the two floors run on different logic. Downstairs is for passing trade: sarongs, batik shirts, wood carvings, basket bags, aimed at the coach crowds who arrive between about eleven and two. Upstairs the same goods often sit at lower prices, because fewer people climb the stairs. Go up.

The first price is not the price. Sellers quote tourists ten times what they would take from a neighbour, and haggling is not rudeness, it is the expected ritual — smile, counter at about a third, meet somewhere in the middle, and walk away cheerfully if you cannot agree. Bring small rupiah notes; nobody has change for Rp 100,000 at eight in the morning.

Understand what is being sold. Batik is cloth decorated by drawing or stamping hot wax onto fabric before dyeing, so the waxed parts resist the colour; it is a craft with centuries of history across Indonesia and Java. The wood carvings come mostly from villages south of here — Mas is the carving village, Celuk does silver, Batuan does painting. Ubud's own specialty was always painting, and we will get to that.

Before the art stalls open, this same building runs a different market entirely. From before dawn the ground floor fills with produce — bananas, snake fruit, chillies, temple flowers — and local families do their real shopping. The art market is for you; the food market is for them. Come early and you will see both.

Now look down at the pavement, because this is the best place on the walk to understand the offerings. A canang sari is the small square tray of woven palm leaf you see everywhere in Bali, holding a few flowers, a pinch of rice, a sliver of banana or biscuit, and a burning stick of incense. Women make them every morning by the hundred. They are set on shrines, on doorsteps, on the dashboards of cars, and on the ground — and the ones on the ground are not for the high gods but for the spirits below, the buta kala, the disruptive forces that must be fed and placated. It is a daily act of gratitude and balance, not a charm. Do not step on one, and do not photograph a woman mid-prayer with the incense lit as if she were an exhibit; a stall is fair game, a person at worship is not.

The market is free to wander. The food section runs from dawn, the art stalls roughly 08:00 to 18:00, and hours thin on quiet days — verify locally. One warning: on Nyepi, Bali's day of silence, the whole island shuts, so buy what you want the day before. Then walk west along Jalan Raya Ubud — jalan means street, raya means main — for about two hundred metres, to the water temple on your right.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter and browse. Everything inside is negotiable; bring small rupiah notes.
stops.openingHours: Food and produce stalls from before dawn; the art stalls roughly 08:00 to 18:00, with some traders closing earlier on quiet days. Closed entirely on Nyepi. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Ground floor is level but the aisles are narrow and crowded, and the upper floor is reached by steep stairs. Not step-free upstairs.
stops.insiderTip: Go upstairs and to the northern end for lower prices and fewer people — most shoppers never climb the stairs. And avoid the crush from about 11:00 to 14:00, when the coach tours arrive.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west along Jalan Raya Ubud for about two hundred metres, past the junction. The lotus pond and the carved brick gate on your right are Pura Taman Saraswati, the water temple.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Marklchaves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Saraswati Temple (Pura Taman Saraswati)
stops.narration:
Stop at the lotus pond. This is Pura Taman Saraswati — pura means temple, taman means garden, and Saraswati is the Hindu goddess of learning, literature and the arts — and it is one of the loveliest pieces of architecture in Ubud. It was designed by the same I Gusti Nyoman Lempad who carved the palace, commissioned by the prince Cokorda Gede Agung Sukawati, and built in 1951 and 1952. So this is not ancient. Ubud's temple-building has never stopped, and the royal family commissioned this one in part to give the town's dancers and musicians a stage.

The first thing to unlearn is what a temple is. In Balinese Hinduism a pura is not a single hall where everyone sits; it is a walled courtyard open to the sky, holding many shrines and pavilions, and only the innermost area is for the gods and the priests. You are welcome in the outer courtyards. The inner gate — the tall, narrow brick-and-stone doorway with the tiered roof, called a kori agung — is for ceremonies. Notice, straight ahead of it, a low wall blocking the path. That is an aling-aling, a deliberate obstacle whose job is to stop evil spirits, said to travel in straight lines, from walking in behind you. Practical superstition, built in stone.

Now the religion, because it is unlike anything in India. At the top sits Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa, also called Acintya — "the inconceivable" — the one supreme god, represented not by an image but by an empty throne, the padmasana, at the holiest corner of the courtyard. Below that one god are the familiar Hindu deities — Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer — and a busy population of local spirits and ancestors. Saraswati, the goddess honoured here, carries a stringed instrument called a veena and a palm-leaf manuscript: music and learning. She is the patron of exactly the thing Ubud sells.

Etiquette matters here, so here it is. Wear a sarong and tie a sash around your waist; if you are not already wearing one, one is usually lent or hired at the entrance. Take your shoes off in the inner courtyard. Never point your feet at a shrine, never stand higher than a priest, and never photograph someone mid-prayer — a temple is someone's church, not a set. Keep your voice down.

Entry has traditionally been free, though some recent visitors report a small entrance fee of roughly Rp 50,000 to 60,000 being introduced, so bring cash and verify at the gate. Hours are roughly 07:00 to 17:00, and the temple is lit for dance performances some evenings. Stand on the bridge over the lotus pond for a minute — frangipani, still water, carved brick — then continue west along Jalan Raya Ubud for about a hundred and fifty metres. The museum gate on the right, set back behind a garden, is next.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Long free, though some recent visitors report a small entrance fee of around Rp 50,000 to 60,000 being introduced. Bring cash and verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 07:00 to 17:00, and again in the evening for dance performances. Verify at the gate, as hours shift with ceremonies.
stops.accessibility: Level walkway across the lotus pond to the outer courtyard, then a few steps through the gates. The inner courtyard is barefoot and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Stand on the bridge at golden hour, when the pond goes still and the carved brick catches the light. Look for the aling-aling wall in front of the inner gate — most visitors walk straight past it without knowing what it is for.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue west along Jalan Raya Ubud for about a hundred and fifty metres. The museum gate on the right, set back behind a garden with a small ticket desk, is Museum Puri Lukisan.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Museum Puri Lukisan
stops.narration:
The gate says Museum Puri Lukisan: puri is palace, lukisan is painting, so "the palace of paintings". When it opened in 1954 it was the first private art museum in Bali, founded by the same Prince Cokorda Gede Agung Sukawati with the Dutch painter Rudolf Bonnet, and its three pavilions hold the story of how Ubud became the art capital of the island.

That story begins in the 1920s and 1930s, and it is stranger than the guidebooks admit. Ubud's royal family, short of money and long on prestige, invited foreign artists to live in the town. Two came and changed everything. Walter Spies was a German painter and musician who arrived in 1927 and became the hinge between Balinese and European art. Rudolf Bonnet was a Dutch painter who arrived in 1929 and stayed for decades. Together with the prince they founded, in 1936, an association called Pita Maha — Balinese for "great ancestor" — to raise the standard of local painting and sell it abroad.

Look at the paintings and you can see the collaboration. Balinese artists had painted flat, decorative, ritual scenes for temple cloths. Under Spies and Bonnet's encouragement they took up Western perspective, shading and individual portraiture while keeping Balinese subjects: market scenes, processions, dancers, rice fields crowded with figures. The result was a hybrid nobody had made before, and Europe and America bought it by the crate. This is the awkward heart of the place: the "Bali" the world fell in love with — the paradise of artists and temples — was partly manufactured here, by a colonial-era friendship between a prince and two Europeans. Ubud did not simply have a culture that tourists discovered; it built a culture for them to discover, and it has been renegotiating that bargain ever since.

There is a darker thread. Bali was under Dutch colonial rule — Ubud had become a Dutch protectorate in 1900, at its own request, to escape a stronger neighbour — and the colonial state criminalised homosexuality. In 1938 Spies was arrested for it and left Bali; he died in 1942 when the ship evacuating him from Java was bombed. Bonnet was interned by the occupying Japanese. The art they made outlived them, and so did the town's dependence on the trade.

Inside, look for the ink drawings of I Gusti Nyoman Lempad — the palace's carver, drawing in the 1930s — and Bonnet's portraits of Balinese sitters, which are the most contested things in the collection: beautiful, and exactly the kind of gaze the word "colonial" was invented for.

Entry is around Rp 40,000; verify at the desk, since prices move and pavilions occasionally close for repair. Hours are roughly 08:00 to 16:00 daily, and the garden café is a good place to sit out the midday heat. Leave, turn left, and walk back east along Jalan Raya Ubud for about four hundred metres to the junction by the palace — then we turn south.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around Rp 40,000, roughly. Prices move and pavilions occasionally close for repair, so verify at the desk.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 08:00 to 16:00. Confirm on the day, as individual pavilions sometimes close.
stops.accessibility: Level garden paths between pavilions with a few low steps at the entrances. The main galleries are manageable; the garden is mostly flat.
stops.insiderTip: Look for I Gusti Nyoman Lempad's ink drawings and Bonnet's portraits — and ask at the desk which pavilion is open, because there is often one closed for repair. The garden café is the coolest place in town at midday.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the museum, walk back east along Jalan Raya Ubud for about four hundred metres to the junction by the palace, then turn right and follow Jalan Monkey Forest south for about two kilometres — roughly twenty-five minutes. The sanctuary gates are at the bottom of the street, where the road ends.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sacred Monkey Forest Sanctuary
stops.narration:
Pay at the gate and step into a jungle with temples in it. This is Mandala Suci Wenara Wana, known to everyone as the Monkey Forest: about ten hectares of forest owned not by the government or a company but by the village of Padangtegal, and run by it. Three Hindu temples stand inside, all built around 1350, and roughly a thousand long-tailed macaques — Macaca fascicularis, the crab-eating macaque — live here in five territorial troops. The count swings year to year, so distrust any guide who gives you an exact figure; the sanctuary's own numbers have run from around 750 to over 1,200.

First the monkeys, because they will find you. These are wild animals that have lost their fear of people, not pets, and the rules exist because bites happen. Do not feed them, do not carry visible food or rustling plastic bags, do not touch them, do not stare into their eyes — in macaque language that is a threat — and if one climbs on you, stand still and let it leave. Staff carry slingshots, not to hit the monkeys but to frighten them off when they get aggressive. The sanctuary once sold bananas to visitors; it stopped, because the monkeys grew fat and demanding.

Now the sacred part, which is why the forest is protected at all. The main temple, in the south-west, is Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal — the Great Temple of Death of the village of Padangtegal — and it honours Shiva, the god who destroys and recycles, the force that turns one life into the next. The north-west temple, Pura Beji, is a holy-spring temple for purification, used for melukat, a cleansing ritual with water. And the north-east temple, Pura Prajapati, stands beside a cemetery where the dead are buried temporarily while they wait for a mass cremation. That is the central rite of Balinese Hinduism: ngaben, cremation, which releases the soul from the body so it can be reborn. Because a proper cremation is expensive, villages often wait and burn many bodies together — the sanctuary's own cemetery holds the dead until the next collective ceremony, which may be years away.

The whole forest runs on a principle worth carrying away from Bali. It is called tri hita karana: three causes of wellbeing — harmony between people and people, people and nature, and people and the divine. It is not a slogan. The village makes real money from the monkeys, this being one of Bali's most-visited attractions, and the income is meant to serve the village and the forest together. Whether that balance holds as visitor numbers climb is the live argument in Ubud, and you are standing inside it.

Some temple areas are closed to visitors, and worshippers have the right of way everywhere. If you enter a temple courtyard you need a sarong and a sash; walk barefoot inside; never stand above someone praying.

Entry is around Rp 130,000 for adults and Rp 100,000 for children; verify at the gate, as prices have risen steeply and are reviewed often. Gates are open roughly 09:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:00. Come early for the animals and the shade. When you leave, take a car or a scooter taxi about two kilometres north-west to the Campuhan bridge — that is roughly half an hour on foot along busy roads, so ride it — and we finish on the ridge above the river.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around Rp 130,000 for adults and Rp 100,000 for children, roughly. Prices have risen steeply and are reviewed often — verify at the gate and carry cash.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 09:00 to 18:00, with last entry at 17:00. Confirm on the day, as hours shift with ceremonies.
stops.accessibility: Mostly gentle forest paths with some steps, slopes and uneven stone. The main loop is walkable for most people; the temple courtyards have steps and require bare feet.
stops.insiderTip: Come at opening time: the macaques are active and the coach crowds have not arrived. Keep bags zipped and out of sight, and watch the stone guardians and the dragon bridge as much as the monkeys.
stops.nextStopDirections: Take a car or a scooter taxi about two kilometres north-west to the Campuhan bridge, at the west end of Jalan Raya Ubud — that is roughly half an hour on foot along busy roads, so ride it. From the bridge, the ridge path begins on the far side, beside the old temple at the foot of the valley.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Campuhan Ridge Walk
stops.narration:
From the bridge, look down. Two rivers meet below you — the two branches of the Wos, the Yeh Wos Kiwa and the Yeh Wos Tengen — and in Balinese Hinduism a river confluence is one of the holiest spots, because two waters becoming one is where the divine comes closest to the world. The temple at the foot of the valley, Pura Gunung Lebah, is at least a thousand years old in its foundations. It was founded, the legend says, by Rsi Markandya, a priest who came from Java in the 8th century, meditated here, and is credited with planting the roots of Balinese Hinduism — Agama Tirta, "the religion of holy water" — across the island. Pilgrims still come to bathe and collect holy water here. And Ubud's name comes from here: ubad is Balinese for medicine, because the valley was famous for healing plants.

Now turn up the path. This is the Campuhan Ridge Walk, a concrete footpath about a metre wide running roughly two kilometres along the spine of a ridge between two river valleys. It is the best place to see what makes the landscape work, so let us talk about rice.

Those terraces are not scenery; they are a machine, and it is a thousand years old. Bali's rice grows in flooded paddies fed by canals, tunnels and small dams, and the system is governed by cooperatives called subak. A subak is a group of farmers who share one water source — between fifty and a few hundred households — and its members elect officers and agree rules; the water temples along the system decide when each subak, upstream and downstream, may open its sluices. There are around 1,200 to 1,500 subak on the island. The clever part is the timing. Everyone in an area plants and floods at the same moment, then lets the fields dry together; the shared fallow starves the pests that would otherwise move from field to field. That is pest control by synchronised calendar, invented centuries before anyone called it ecology. In 2012 UNESCO listed the subak system as a World Heritage Site.

It has nearly died twice. In 1971 the Indonesian government pushed the "Green Revolution" here: new fast-growing rice, fertilisers, pesticides, three crops a year. Farmers were pushed to plant continuously, the coordinated calendar collapsed, and by the late 1970s pests were destroying up to half the crop. By 1988 the government reversed course and handed water scheduling back to the subak. The second threat is the one you are walking through. Rice land near the towns is worth more as villa sites, and Bali loses roughly a thousand hectares of farmland a year; hotels and villas now consume most of the island's freshwater. Supporters call it renewal and jobs; critics say tourism is eating the thing tourists came for.

One more thing, because you may be here for it. Nyepi, the Balinese New Year, falls on 8 March 2027, and it shuts the whole island down for twenty-four hours from six in the morning. The airport closes. Everyone, visitors included, stays indoors. Lights stay dim, no one travels, nothing is sold. The four prohibitions are no fire or light, no work, no travel and no entertainment, and the point is to make Bali look empty so the demons roaming on new year's eve pass the island by. The night before, villages parade ogoh-ogoh — towering demon effigies of bamboo and paper — through the streets and burn them. Tourists are welcome at the parades and bound by the silence that follows, enforced by the pecalang, the village security force. The day after, Ngembak Geni, the island wakes up and asks forgiveness all round.

Stand here a while. Everything under the light — the water, the rice, the temples — is held together by cooperation, not by accident. That is the end of the walk.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The path is public; the temple at the foot of the ridge may ask for a small donation if it is open for worshippers.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times, though the path is unlit and best walked in daylight — early morning or the hour before sunset. Closed to walkers on Nyepi.
stops.accessibility: A narrow concrete path, about a metre wide, with a steady climb and no shade at midday. Not suitable for wheelchairs, and the drop to the valleys is unfenced in places.
stops.insiderTip: Walk it at sunrise or in the last hour of light — the path bakes at midday with no shade. The far end reaches a café about two kilometres on, or turn back to the bridge; either way, look down at the confluence before you start.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. The path runs on about two kilometres to a café at the far end, or you can turn back to the bridge in twenty minutes. From the Campuhan bridge, Jalan Raya Ubud is two minutes away, with cafés, taxis and scooter-hailing apps, and the palace and market are a ten-minute walk east. If it is dark, take a car rather than walking the unlit path back. And if your visit falls on Nyepi, be indoors well before dawn — the whole island, and the airport, shut for twenty-four hours.
